1. The animation compares two borrowers, Leo and Tessa. Each has a house, a gold stack of coins, and a bar showing their loan's own interest rate. The data source is labeled as the Freddie Mac weekly mortgage survey. The comparison seems to be between a 15-year and a 30-year mortgage. The caption says the stack shows how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit. The whole thing is marked "illustrative", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. Mostly the on-screen captions change. They build up one line at a time, from "your bar = your loan's own rate" to "your stack = how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit". Frame 6 adds "a dollar in the house is hard to get back". A dashed outline box and a dashed bar are also highlighted. The house shading changes slightly. In frame 6 Tessa's house has more green fill than in the earlier frames. The people and the bars stay in place.

3. The likely meaning is that the interest rate you get on your mortgage sets what an extra dollar of payment earns you. That rate is the return you lock in by paying the loan down. The gap between 15-year and 30-year rates is shown as a stack. Money put into the house, such as extra principal or equity, is also hard to get out again. It's less liquid than money you invest elsewhere. The frames don't show any numbers. I'm interpreting the pictures and captions, and some of this is a guess.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer could take away that your own loan's rate matters when deciding between extra payments and investing. They could also take away that money put into the house is harder to recover. The "history, not a forecast" label warns against reading it as a prediction. It doesn't say which choice is better.

5. Part of it came from the animation and part is my own conclusion. The captions say your bar is your loan's rate and that a dollar in the house is hard to get back. Those lines hint at the considerations a viewer might weigh. The "pay extra versus invest" framing, and any idea that the viewer should do one or the other, are not in the image. I took that framing from your question, and the animation doesn't state it.
